title: Dissolving the Pain-Body
excerpt: By Eckhart Tolle; translated by Zhang Defen.

inline.s: Excerpted from Practicing the Power of Now.
By Eckhart Tolle
Translated by Zhang Defen.
The intensity of your pain depends on the degree to which you resist the present moment;
and the degree to which you resist the present moment, in turn, depends on the degree to which you identify with your mind.

Editor’s note: A sickness of the heart must be cured with the medicine of the heart. Whenever you feel resentment, hatred, self-pity, guilt, anger, depression, envy, irritation, despondency, or sheer boredom, set this text beside you and listen to it carefully once through. Then dwell on it for a while and do as it says. At first, do as much as you can. Once it begins to work, you will naturally find your way.

Most human suffering is unnecessary. It is self-created, because the unobserved mind runs your life. The pain you create now is always some form of nonacceptance of what is, some form of unconscious resistance.

On the level of thought, resistance is some form of criticism; on the level of emotion, it is some form of negativity. The intensity of your pain depends on the degree to which you resist the present moment; and the degree of that resistance depends on the degree to which you identify with your mind. For the mind always tries to deny the present moment and flee from it.

[Mind] The thinking of the head, the thinker. In the original of this book the word for “mind” is mind. [Identification with the mind] To believe that the mind (the thinker) is truly who you are. At the very opening this book says: “The first taste of freedom comes from realizing that you are not the thinker.”

In other words, the more you identify with your mind, the more you suffer. Or you could say it this way: the more you are able to honor and accept the present moment, the more you are set free from pain and from being a victim — that is, free from the mind of the ego.

Some spiritual teachings point out that all pain is ultimately an illusion, and this is true. The question is: is it true for you? Mere belief does not make it true. Are you willing to spend your whole life experiencing pain, while constantly telling yourself that it is only an illusion? Does doing so set you free from pain? What concerns us here is how you can put the truth into practice — that is, how you can verify, in your own experience, that “all pain is ultimately an illusion” is true.

As long as you identify with the mind, pain is unavoidable. That is, as long as you are unconscious (in the spiritual sense), you cannot escape pain. What I refer to here is mainly emotional pain, which is likewise the principal cause of physical pain and illness. Resentment, hatred, self-pity, guilt, anger, depression, envy, and so on — even the slightest irritation — are all forms of pain in various guises.

Every kind of pleasure or emotional high contains within it the seed of pain: its inseparable opposite, and that opposite will sooner or later manifest. Anyone who has ever tried drugs to get high knows that the high eventually turns into a low, that pleasure turns into some form of pain. Many people also know from their own experience how easily and how quickly an intimate relationship turns from a source of joy into a source of pain. From a higher vantage, the positive and negative poles are two sides of the same coin, and both are part of the underlying pain of each one of us, and that underlying pain is inseparable from the ego-consciousness that identifies with the mind.
Your pain has two levels: first, the pain you create now; and second, the old pain that is still alive in your mind and body.

As long as you cannot access the power of the present moment, every emotional pain you experience leaves a residue behind that continues to live within you. It merges with the old pain already present from the past, and dwells long within your mind and body. This, of course, includes the pain you suffered in childhood, which was brought about by the unconsciousness of the world into which you were born.
This accumulated pain forms a field of negative energy that occupies your body and mind. If you regard it as an invisible entity, you are not far from the truth. This is the emotional pain-body.

The pain-body has two modes of being: dormant and active. It may be dormant more than ninety percent of the time, yet in a profoundly unhappy person the pain-body may be active a full hundred percent of the time. Some people live almost entirely through their pain-body, while others experience it only in certain situations — for example, in an intimate relationship, or in situations connected with past loss or abandonment, with physical or emotional trauma, and so on.

Anything can trigger the pain-body, especially when something resonates with your past pain pattern. When the pain-body is ready to wake from its dormant state, even a thought or a careless remark from someone nearby can stir it.

Above all, the pain-body fears you observing it directly and seeing it for what it truly is. When you observe your own pain-body, sense its energy field within you, and turn your attention into it, that identification collapses.

Then a higher dimension of consciousness enters, which I call presence. You have now become the witness or observer of the pain-body. This means it can no longer use you by pretending to be you, nor can it feed itself through you. You have found your own deepest strength.

Some pain-bodies are like a child crying without cease — very disagreeable, but by comparison fairly harmless. Some pain-bodies are evil and destructive monsters — true demons. Some incline toward physical violence, but many more toward emotional violence. Some attack the people around you or those close to you, while others attack you, who are their host. When you are under attack by a pain-body, your thoughts and feelings about your own life become extremely negative and self-destructive. Illness and accidents are often produced in just this way. Some pain-bodies even drive their host to suicide.

[Host] A plant, animal, or person on which a parasite — a virus, bacterium, spirochete, fungus, protozoan, insect, or the like — lives. The parasite dwells within or on the surface of the host’s body, drawing nourishment from it, and often harms the host, making it ill or even killing it.

Sometimes you think you know someone very well, but all of a sudden you are face to face with a strange, disagreeable monster. The first time this happens you may well be badly startled. Yet observing the pain-body within yourself is more important than seeing it in another person.

Watch for any sign of unhappiness within yourself, in whatever form — that is very likely a pain-body waking up. It will take many forms: irritation, impatience, a sullen mood, a desire to hurt someone, anger, rage, depression, or the urge to create drama in a relationship, and so on. Catch it the very moment it is waking from its dormant phase.

Like every existing entity, the pain-body wants to keep surviving, yet it can survive only through your unconsciously identifying with it. When you do so, the pain-body rises up, takes you over, becomes you, and then lives on through you.

The pain-body needs to get its “food” through you. It feeds on any experience that resonates with its own particular frequency, anything that can further manufacture pain, in whatever form: anger, destruction, hatred, sorrow, emotional drama, violence, even illness. Once the pain-body has taken you over, it creates a situation in your life that radiates energy of the same frequency, so as to feed itself. Pain can feed only on pain. It cannot feast on joy; joy is indigestible to it.

Once the pain-body has taken you over, you want more pain. You become either a victim or a persecutor. You either want to inflict pain on others, or you want to suffer yourself, or both — and the two are in fact not much different. Of course, you are quite unaware of this, and will insist strongly that you do not want pain. But if you look carefully, you will find that your thinking and your behavior are causing continuing suffering to yourself and to others. If you truly became aware of this, the pattern would dissolve, for behavior that wants more pain is madness, and no one would consciously choose to do something mad.

The pain-body is the black shadow cast by the ego; it is in truth very much afraid of your light of consciousness, very much afraid of being seen. The pain-body’s survival depends on your unconsciously identifying with it, and on your unconsciously fearing to face the pain living within you. But if you do not face your pain, if you do not bring the light of consciousness into it, you will be compelled to experience it again and again.
To you the pain-body may seem like a dangerous monster that you dare not even look straight at. But I can assure you that it is only a frail phantom, powerless against the strength of your presence.

When you become the observer and begin to dis-identify, the pain-body will still operate for a while, and will try to trick you into identifying with it again. Although you no longer give it energy through identification, the pain-body still has a certain momentum to keep running for a time, like a spinning wheel that, even when it loses its power, keeps turning for a while before it comes to a stop. At this stage it may still cause some pain and discomfort in various parts of the body, but it will not last long.

Stay present, stay conscious, and at every moment vigilantly guard your inner space. You must be present enough to observe the pain-body directly and to feel its energy, so that it cannot take control of your thoughts.

Once your way of thinking is in tune with the pain-body’s energy field, you will identify with it and once again feed it with your thoughts. For instance, if anger is the main energy vibration of your pain-body, and you harbor angry thoughts, forever dwelling on what someone did to you or on what you will do to them, then you have already entered an unconscious state, and the pain-body has become “you.” So whenever anger arises, it is secretly the pain-body operating.

Or when a depressed mood comes over you and you begin to enter a negative mode of thinking, feeling that your life is utterly wretched, then your thinking has already aligned with the pain-body, and you become oblivious and vulnerable to the pain-body’s attacks.
What I mean here by “unconsciousness” is identification with some psychological or emotional pattern. It means the total absence of the observer.

Sustained and conscious attention can cut the connection between the pain-body and your thinking process, and thereby bring about transformation. It is as if the pain became fuel for the flame of your consciousness, so that the flame of consciousness burns all the more brightly.

This is the mystery of the ancient art of alchemy: base metal transformed into gold, suffering transformed into consciousness. The inner split is healed, and you become whole once again. After this, your responsibility is to create no more suffering.

Focus your attention on the feeling within you, recognize it as the pain-body, and accept the fact that it is there. Do not think about it — do not let the feeling turn into thinking; do not criticize or analyze; do not seek your identity (your sense of self) from the pain-body. Stay present, and keep observing what is happening within you.

Not only must you be aware of the emotional pain, you must also be aware of the observer — the silent witness. This is the power of the present moment, the power of your own conscious presence. From there, simply watch the matter unfold.

blocks.text: 5. The Ego’s Identification with the Pain-Body

inline.s: The process I have just described is, so to speak, powerful and far-reaching, and yet utterly simple — so simple that even a child could learn it. I hope that one day it will be among the first things a child is taught in school. Once you have understood, through your own experience, the basic principle of staying present (presence is to observe what is happening within), you hold the most powerful tool of transformation and can use it at will.

This is not to deny that you may encounter strong inner resistance — resistance to withdrawing from your pain. Especially if you have closely identified with your emotional pain-body for most of your life, and have invested all or most of your sense of self in it, this resistance will arise. It means you have manufactured an unhappy self out of the pain-body, and believe that this mental construct is truly who you are. In such a case, an unconscious fear of losing your identity creates powerful resistance against withdrawing from this identification. In other words, you would rather remain in pain — be the pain-body — than take the risk of losing the familiar, unhappy self and leap into the unknown.

Observe the resistance within yourself; observe your attachment to your pain; stay highly alert. Observe the strange pleasure you derive from being unhappy, and observe the compulsive urge to talk about or to think about it. If you become aware of it, that resistance will disappear.
Only then can you bring your attention into the pain-body, and be present there as an observer, thereby setting the pain-body’s transformation in motion.

Only you can do this; no one else can do it for you. But if you are fortunate enough to find highly conscious people, and to stay with them and enter into their presence, it will be a great help and will accelerate the process of transformation. In this way your light of consciousness will grow quickly and thrive.

When a piece of wood just beginning to catch fire is placed alongside a piece that is already blazing, after a while, even when the two are separated again, the first piece burns more fiercely than before, for the fire is the same. One of the functions of a spiritual teacher is to be that blazing piece of wood. Some psychotherapists can serve the same function, provided that in their therapy they can go beyond the psychological level and create and maintain a state of high conscious presence.

The first thing to remember is this: as long as you make your identity out of your pain, you cannot be free of it; as long as you invest part of your sense of self in emotional pain, you will unconsciously resist or undermine any attempt to heal that wound.

Why? Very simply, because the pain has become a major part of who you are, and you want to keep yourself whole. This is an unconscious process, and the only way to overcome it is to become aware of it.
To suddenly discover that you have been attached to your own pain may come as quite a surprise. But in the very moment you realize it, you have already broken that attachment.
The pain-body is an energy field, almost like an entity, dwelling within your inner space. It is trapped life-energy that has ceased to flow.

Of course, the pain-body exists because of certain things that happened in the past; it is the past living within you, and if you identify with it, you identify with the past. A victim identity is the belief that the past is more powerful than the present, which is the opposite of the truth. You believe that other people and what they did to you should be responsible for the kind of person you are now, and for your emotional pain or your inability to become your true self.

In fact, the only power that exists is the one inherent in this very moment — the power of your presence. Once you understand this, you will also understand that you are responsible for your inner space at this moment — that this is no one else’s responsibility — and that the past can never prevail over the power of the present.

Unconsciousness created the pain-body, and consciousness transforms it into consciousness itself. St. Paul gave beautiful expression to this universal truth: “In the light all things are laid bare; and whatever is made manifest by the light becomes light.”

Just as you cannot fight against darkness, so too you cannot fight the pain-body. Trying to do so only creates inner conflict and brings about more pain. To observe it is enough. To “observe it” means to accept it, in that very moment, as part of what is.
